subject: physics
title: Half-life
key_idea: Radioactive decay is random, so we cannot say when one nucleus will decay. In a large sample the **half-life** is the time for the activity, or the number of undecayed nuclei, to halve. After each half-life the amount left is half of what it was.

blocks.text: Each unstable nucleus decays at a random time. This section covers what that means and how half-life describes a whole sample.

items.meaning: It cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay.
The time for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or for the count rate (activity) of the sample to fall to half its initial level.
The rate at which a source decays, measured in becquerel (Bq).

items: We cannot predict when any one nucleus will decay.
A sample has a very large number of nuclei, so its activity can be predicted using the half-life.
The activity of a source falls over time as nuclei decay.
A short half-life means the activity falls quickly. A long half-life means it falls slowly.
A bigger chance of decay in a given time means a shorter half-life.
Because decay is random, count-rate readings scatter around the expected value.
The scatter is more pronounced at low count rates.
Counting for longer gives a larger count and less variation in the count rate.
Decay is random for a single nucleus, but predictable for a very large number.
Half-life is the time for the activity or the number of undecayed nuclei to halve.

sections.heading: Half-life from a graph or data

blocks.text: The activity of a source falls in a curve. Each half-life takes it down to half of its value.

diagram.alt: A decay curve: activity halves every half-life, so it falls steeply at first and then more slowly.

items.text: Pick an activity or count rate on the graph, or in the table.
Work out half of that value.
Find the time at which each value occurs.
The difference in time is one half-life. Check with a second starting value.

blocks.text: Move the slider to see how many nuclei are left. Here the half-life is 10 minutes.

diagram.alt: Change the time and see how many nuclei of a sample with a 10 minute half-life are left.

outputs.label: Nuclei left, from 100 at the start

blocks.text: The diagram shows the expected number. In a real sample the numbers vary a little, because decay is random.

items: The activity halves in every half-life, giving a curve that falls steeply and then flattens.
Read a half-life as the time taken for any value on the curve to halve.

sections.heading: Calculating after a number of half-lives

blocks.text: First find how many half-lives have passed. Then halve the starting value that many times.

blocks.label: Number of half-lives
where: time and half-life are in the same unit, for example days.

blocks.label: Amount remaining
where: initial is the starting number of nuclei, mass or activity.
n is the number of half-lives.

items.text: A sample with a half-life of 12 hours is left for 36 hours. n = 36 ÷ 12 = 3.
A count rate of 640 counts per minute becomes 320, then 160, then 80.
The count rate after 36 hours is 80 counts per minute, which is 640 × (½)³.

items: To work backwards to the starting value, double the final value once for each half-life.
The activity after n half-lives is (½)ⁿ of the start. After 3 half-lives, one-eighth is left.

blocks.text: (AQA: Higher tier) The net decline can be written as a ratio. After n half-lives, the final activity to the initial activity is 1 : 2ⁿ. After 3 half-lives this is 1 : 8.

diagram.alt: Calculate a count rate after several half-lives of iodine-131.
diagram.question: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample has a count rate of {A0} counts per minute. Calculate its count rate after {t} days.
working: Count rate = {A0} × (½) to the power of the number of half-lives

items: Number of half-lives = time ÷ half-life.
Halve the starting value once for each half-life.
(AQA: Higher tier) After n half-lives the ratio of final to initial activity is 1 : 2ⁿ.

blocks.text: The half-life of an isotope decides how long its radiation stays a hazard and how useful it is.

items: For the same number of nuclei, the isotope with the shorter half-life has the higher activity at the start.
A short half-life means the activity, and so the risk of harm, decreases quickly.
A long half-life means the activity hardly changes over a short time. Radon-222 has a half-life of 3.8 days, so its activity is almost unchanged after 7.4 minutes.
Vanadium-52 has a half-life of 3.7 minutes. After 7.4 minutes, 2 half-lives have passed and its activity has decreased by a factor of 4.
A source that must last for a long time needs a long half-life, so that it does not run out.
The shorter the half-life, the higher the starting activity and the faster the risk falls.
A long half-life means the source lasts and the hazard stays for a long time.

checks.q: Define the half-life of a radioactive isotope.
checks.a: The time taken for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or for the activity (count rate) from the sample to fall to half its initial level.

checks.q: A source has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 6 hours. Calculate its activity after 18 hours.
Two samples have the same number of nuclei. One has a half-life of 2 years and the other 400 years. Which has the higher activity at the start?
checks.a: The one with the half-life of 2 years. A shorter half-life means more decays each second.

worked_example.question:
Polonium-210 has a half-life of 138 days. A sample of polonium contains 256 000 atoms.

Calculate the time taken for the number of polonium-210 atoms to reach 16 000.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the number of half-lives, one for multiplying by the half-life and one for the answer, 552 days.

worked_example.question:
The half-life of cobalt-60 is 5 years.

A school cobalt source had an activity of 38.5 kBq in the year 2000.

Estimate the activity of this source in the year 2020.
answer_points: Recognition that 4 half-lives are involved (20 years ÷ 5 years).
So a fraction of 1/16 is involved.
worked_example.tip: The correct answer without working scores full marks. Another power of (½) scores 1 mark.

worked_example.question:
A technician investigates a radioactive metal, metal D, which emits gamma radiation and has a half-life of 28 days.

Metal D is considered to be safe when the count rate drops to 1/32 of the original count rate.

Calculate the time required for metal D to be safe.

Time required = ______ days
worked_example.tip: A correct answer of 140 on the answer line scores all 3 marks. Halving something 5 times (1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8 → 1/16 → 1/32) is also credited.

worked_example.question:
A radiation detector used in a laboratory detects a background count rate of 30 counts / min.

A radioactive source is placed in front of the radiation detector. The initial reading on the detector is 550 counts / min. The half-life of the source is 25 minutes.

Calculate the expected reading on the detector after 75 minutes.
answer_points: Initial count rate from the source = 550 - 30 = 520 counts / min.
75 minutes is 3 half-lives, so the count rate falls to 1/8.
Final count rate from the source = 520 ÷ 8 = 65 counts / min.
Reading on the detector = 65 + 30 = 95 counts / min.
worked_example.tip: The background count is not halved, so take it away first and add it back at the end.

blocks.text: (Supplement) A reading or decay curve may include background radiation. Subtract the background first, then find the half-life from the corrected values.

items.text: Subtract the background count rate from every reading.
Find the time for the corrected count rate to fall to half.
To find an expected reading, add the background to the answer.

worked_example.question:
Uranium-235 decays to thorium-231 with a half-life of 700 million years.

When a rock was formed, it contained 6400 million uranium-235 nuclei and no thorium-231 nuclei.

Show that after 2100 million years there are seven times more thorium nuclei than uranium nuclei in the rock.
answer_points: After 1 half-life there are 3200 million uranium nuclei; after 3 half-lives there are 800 million.
5600 ÷ 800 = 7, so there are seven times more thorium nuclei.

blocks.text: Nuclear reactions can be a source of energy. This includes radioactive decay as well as fission and fusion. The half-life tells you how quickly a decaying source gives out its energy.
